kept.spine: Nothing presses the town at present, and the quiet is not luck. A place kept this ready costs more to try than it is worth.
The country outside is frontier, and what is in it is known here and talked of nowhere. The walls are kept up, and the garrison is paid to stand behind them.
faces: A drover says he is asked at the gate what he carries and never what he came past on the road.
The men who hold the ways in say the bar goes down at dusk, and whoever is late sleeps outside the wall.
A priest of one of the parishes holds that the walls have the town's thanks and the almshouse behind them has what is left.
One of the aldermen says the hall pays for the walls and hears nothing back from the country but quiet.
The watch says a complaint about the nights is made to it at the gate and goes no further.
At one of the taverns a carter says the talk is all of who stands the nights, and the country itself never comes up.
A soldier of the garrison says the town never comes out to watch a drill and never asks what the drilling is for.
A warden of one of the guilds reckons the trades pay the toll at the gates and the whole town takes the credit for the walls.
The stallholders say the stalls go up whatever is loose in the country, and that a frontier is a word for people who do not sell.
A clerk of one of the courts holds that a dispute over the toll is heard the day it is brought, and the country brings none.
The elders say the young stand the nights and the old say how they are stood.

kept.poolKey: Invasion & War: walls AND professional garrison
kept.spine: A traveller is stopped at the gate and counted before he is let through. What he is let into is a town that keeps a garrison of its own.
faces: A gatekeeper says a stranger pays where he is stopped and the hall is settled with later, in the gate's own time.
A woman who keeps the hall books says a stranger who pays at the gate has paid the town, and that the men there are not the town.
The officers of the court hold that anyone who paid the toll may argue it there, a stranger as readily as a carter.
A traveller says his pack is opened at the gate and nothing is taken out of it but the toll.
A woman at the long table says the town is never asked whether it wants soldiers, only what they cost.

kept.spine: The law here has a court and no cell. What the court can take from a man is his money or his place in the town.
faces: A night patrolman says what he comes across after dark is settled after dark, there being nowhere to leave a man until morning.
A bailiff says the court hears in daylight what the watch settled in the dark and is not asked first.
A clerk in the hall reckons the purse has never run to a cell and that the court manages without one.
A stallholder says a short weight goes before the court and comes back as a sum, and the scales stay on the stall.
A parish warden holds that the parish has a place for a man once he is dead and the town has none for him alive.
A journeyman says a fine is paid out of a man's takings and forgotten, and the same is never true of his name.
The drinkers of the district say a man with a house here pays and stays, and a man without one is walked to the gate.
A pilgrim says there is nothing here to take from a man who owns nothing, and the town is left with only the road.
A man on one of the gates says he is handed a person and a direction and no reason for either.
A soldier of the garrison says what comes at the town is his to answer for and what is walked out of it is the court's.

kept.spine: Everyone in the town has seen the grain store kept full, and takes it that a crisis would find the place ready.
faces: The mayor says the town asks the trades for no more than the trades can carry.
A warden of one of the guilds says the carrying is theirs and the asking is not.
The guilds' account is the likelier, the hall having a purse to defend and the guilds only a bill.
One of the watch says the rounds are walked by people who are owed for walking them.
A gatekeeper says a cart bound for the grain store goes through ahead of whatever else is waiting at the gate.
A rider who stopped a night says the grain store is praised and the wage complained of by the same people.
An innkeeper says the watch is a trade that drinks on what it is owed.
A man who draws the wage says a town that can be fed through a crisis and still pays him short has decided something, and has not said what.
The traders at the fair say the hall is settled with before anybody settles anything of their own.
The parish clerks hold that the town keeps its word to the dead before it keeps its word to the living.

kept.poolKey: Disasters & Famine: granary AND parish care only
kept.spine: A grain store is kept here and the place looks provided for from outside. No sick house stands in the town, and whoever tends the sick comes out of the church.
faces: A priest of one of the parishes says a stranger asking for a sick house is given the name of a person.
A porter in the square reckons grain is hard to keep here for anybody without a door of his own.
A potboy of the district says strangers ask him the way to the grain store and never ask him after the sick.
The watch says strangers ask it where the grain is kept and nobody has ever asked it where the sick are.
The guild master holds that what a stranger takes for plenty is a store the trades filled and cannot open.
A clerk of the court says a stranger's questions about the store are ordinary and his questions about the sick are new here.

kept.spine: Rundgate runs on a working balance. Its safer streets and its exposed ones are a short walk apart, and neither the law nor the crime has the run of the town.

kept.poolKey: First-Survey qualification (the reading is a first look)
kept.spine: The safety here rests on a first look. The quiet corners after dark are where a first look stops.
A stranger here is not robbed, and somebody takes him aside to tell him the arrangement.
The town holds every way into itself. The walls and gates are what let it choose where anything happens.
Defending this place is somebody's trade and not somebody's turn. The garrison and the city watch draw a wage for the work and answer for the work.
Some of the men who fight for this town are hired, and the town knows which ones. The mercenary quarter keeps its own streets, and the town deals with it the way it deals with a trade.
The kind of trouble a garrison is the wrong tool against has its own trade here. The adventurers' guilds keep more than one house in this town and none of them is quiet.
Whoever comes in at the gate is looked over in a way he cannot put a name to, and nobody offers him the name.
The city walls and gates are in better repair than the watch that stands on them is paid. The upkeep of the stone and the wage come out of one purse, and the wage comes last.

kept.poolKey: Logistics & Supply: Granary with road supply
kept.spine: The town keeps a grain store and is fed by the roads and by no water. What the store buys, if the roads are cut, is time.
